paragraphs.heading: From solid to liquid
paragraphs.text: Melting, also known as fusion, is the change of a substance from a solid into a liquid. It happens when the energy stored inside the solid goes up, most often because heat or pressure is applied, and this lifts its temperature to the melting point. At that temperature, the neat arrangement of ions or molecules in the solid gives way to a looser, less ordered state, and the solid turns into a liquid.

paragraphs.heading: What changes at the melting point
paragraphs.text: In thermodynamics, melting is described using a quantity called Gibbs free energy. A solid melts once the liquid form of the material has a lower Gibbs free energy than the solid form. At the melting point itself, the change in Gibbs free energy is zero, yet the enthalpy (H) and the entropy (S) both change. These changes are named the enthalpy of fusion, also called the latent heat of fusion, and the entropy of fusion. That is why melting is classed as a first-order phase transition, and the temperature where it happens depends on the surrounding pressure.

paragraphs.heading: Helium melts the other way
paragraphs.text: Usually a solid melts when heat is added to it. Helium at very low temperatures is the only known exception. Helium-3 has a negative enthalpy of fusion below 0.3 K, and helium-4 has a very slightly negative one below 0.8 K. In practice, at suitable constant pressures, heat has to be taken away from these substances to make them melt.

paragraphs.heading: Why crystals give way
paragraphs.text: Two theoretical criteria are used most often to analyse when melting happens: the Lindemann criterion and the Born criterion. The Lindemann criterion blames vibrational instability, so a crystal melts once its atoms shake with an average amplitude that is large next to the distances between them. Experimental data back this idea for crystals and also for the glass-liquid transition in amorphous materials. The Born criterion looks at rigidity instead. When the elastic shear modulus vanishes, the crystal can no longer stand up to a mechanical load, and it becomes a liquid.

paragraphs.heading: Colder than freezing, still liquid
paragraphs.text: Under a standard set of conditions, each substance has its own characteristic melting point, which is often the same as its freezing point. With careful preparation, though, a substance can be supercooled or superheated past that point. Water on a very clean glass surface often stays liquid several degrees below its freezing point, and fine emulsions of pure water have been taken to −38 °C without ice forming. The change starts with nucleation, which comes from fluctuations in the material's properties, and a material kept still may have nothing, such as a vibration, to set it off. In thermodynamic terms, a supercooled liquid is in a metastable state compared with the crystal, and it tends to crystallize all at once.

paragraphs.heading: Melting before the melting point
paragraphs.text: Even below the melting point, liquid-like films, called quasi-liquid films, can be seen on the surfaces of crystals. How thick they are depends on the temperature, and the effect is common to all crystalline materials. This pre-melting shows up in frost heave and in the growth of snowflakes. Once the boundaries between crystal grains are taken into account, it may even play a part in how glaciers move.

paragraphs.heading: Melting without heating the atoms
paragraphs.text: In the physics of ultrashort laser pulses, a material can undergo what is called nonthermal melting. Here the cause is not faster-moving atoms but a change in the interatomic potential brought on by exciting the electrons. Electrons behave like a glue that holds atoms together. Heating the electrons with a femtosecond laser alters that glue, which can break the bonds between atoms and melt the material even though the atoms themselves have not got hotter.
